stem: Priya Raman sees performers as healthy learners who struggle mostly because nobody has shown them the right techniques, and she sees her own role as that of an instructor. At a first meeting, collegiate swimmer Tomasz Wójcik says he isn't sure what to expect and asks, "So how does this work?" Which explanation is most consistent with Priya's philosophy of practice?
options: "You'll lead our talks, and my part is to understand your experience as you see it."
"We'll look for races that already go well, and you'll do more of what works in them."
"I'll teach you a set sequence of skills, and you'll practice them between our meetings."
"We'll look at how you interpret your races, and you'll test whether those readings hold up."
rationales: This is a person-centered explanation. It suits a consultant who trusts clients to find their own direction when deeply understood, but Priya sees clients as lacking techniques and herself as the one who supplies them.
Building on existing successes is solution-focused and assumes the swimmer already has workable solutions. Priya's stated belief is that performers have not yet been shown the techniques they need.

An educational, skills-training process follows directly from Priya's beliefs: the difficulty is untaught technique, so the instructor teaches and the learner practices. A consultant's philosophy should show in the process and roles described to a new client.
Examining and testing interpretations is cognitive-behavioral and locates the difficulty in how events are read. Priya locates it in techniques nobody has taught.
takeaway: Beliefs about why people struggle and what the consultant is for should show in how the process is explained.

topic: Feminist view of the consulting relationship
stem: Lena Okafor's practice is grounded in feminist approaches, and she regards a consultant's hidden authority as a problem in its own right. She begins work with Marisol Vega, an elite rugby player who says earlier consultants "acted neutral, so I could never tell where they were coming from or why they picked what we did." Which first-session action best puts Lena's view of the working relationship into practice?
options: State for Marisol the values and beliefs that shape how she works as a consultant
Reflect Marisol's feelings back to her without steering where the session goes
Ask Marisol to describe recent matches in which she performed closer to her hopes
Map the people and settings around Marisol that bear on how she performs
rationales: Feminist approaches reject the idea of a value-free helper and use transparency and purposeful self-disclosure to reduce the power difference. It also answers what Marisol found missing: knowing where a consultant stands.
Nondirective reflection is central to person-centered work. Here it would leave Lena's own position just as hidden as that of the consultants who "acted neutral."
Looking for exceptions is a solution-focused move. It may be useful later, but it does nothing about the concealed authority that Lena and Marisol have both named.
Mapping surrounding settings expresses an ecological view of the performer. The stem asks about the relationship between the two of them, where the concern is the consultant's unstated position.
takeaway: In feminist work, openness about the consultant's own values is a way to share power.

stem: A youth soccer academy asks Daniel Whitfield to help a 12-year-old whose play has dropped since January. Working from Bronfenbrenner's ecological model, Daniel learns that she gets on well with her coach, teammates, and parents, that her parents and coach talk often and agree, and that local support for girls' soccer is strong. What changed in January was a hospital's decision to move her mother to night shifts, which has upset the family's week. When Daniel explains his thinking to her parents, at which level should he place the origin of this change?
options: The microsystem, the settings she takes part in and the people in them
The mesosystem, the connections among the settings she takes part in
The macrosystem, the customs and beliefs of the culture she lives in
The exosystem, a setting she isn't part of that still affects her life
rationales: The effect is felt in her home, which is a microsystem, but her relationships in each setting are sound. The question is where the change began, and that was in a workplace she is not part of.
Connections between her settings, such as home and club, are working: her parents and coach talk often and agree. The change began elsewhere.
Cultural beliefs form the macrosystem, and the stem describes strong local support for girls' soccer. A staffing decision at one hospital is not a cultural custom.

A parent's workplace is the classic exosystem: the player does not take part in it, yet its decisions reach her through home. Naming the origin helps Daniel focus the discussion on the family's schedule rather than on faults in the girl, her coach, or her parents.
takeaway: Ecological levels depend on the person's place in the setting: in it, between settings, outside it, or surrounded by it.

topic: Explaining a cognitive model at intake
stem: At intake, professional golfer Hiroshi Tanaka says the walk to the first tee is miserable: he is certain he will shank his opening drive in front of the gallery, though he can't recall when he last did. His consultant, Anika Brandt, works from Beck's cognitive model. When Hiroshi asks what they will actually do about the first tee, which explanation is most consistent with that model?
options: "We'll practice letting the dread be there while you commit to the shot in front of you."
"We'll write down what you expect will happen and compare it with what does happen."
"We'll find first tees where you felt steadier and work out what you did differently there."
"We'll build a breathing routine that settles your body in the minutes before you swing."
rationales: Making room for dread while committing to action describes acceptance-based work such as Mindfulness-Acceptance-Commitment. Beck's model works on the content and accuracy of his forecast.

Beck's model holds that appraisals such as Hiroshi's certainty of a shank drive his distress, and treats them as hypotheses to check against evidence. Recording a forecast and comparing it with the outcome is that collaborative empiricism in action.
Searching for times the problem was smaller is solution-focused. It sidesteps the forecast that Beck's model would make the target.
A breathing routine matches bodily tension. Hiroshi describes a prediction rather than physical symptoms, and Beck's cognitive model would address that prediction.
takeaway: Cognitive work treats a client's forecast as a hypothesis to check against evidence.

stem: Executive Olivia Grant dreads presenting to her board and asks consultant Hollis Penrose how their sessions will run. He replies, "I won't try to talk you out of the dread or wait for it to fade. We'll get clear on the kind of leader you want to be in that room, and you'll practice presenting that way with the dread along for the ride." Which theoretical orientation does Hollis's explanation best reflect?
options: Rogers's person-centered counseling approach
Hayes's acceptance and commitment therapy
Beck's cognitive behavior therapy
De Shazer's solution-focused brief therapy
rationales: Person-centered work would leave the direction to Olivia and rely on the relationship. Hollis lays out a plan of his own: clarify how she wants to lead, then practice it while the dread is present.
Letting the dread remain (acceptance), clarifying how she wants to lead (values), and presenting that way anyway (committed action) are core processes of acceptance and commitment therapy.
Cognitive behavior therapy would examine and test the thoughts behind the dread. Hollis says outright that he won't try to change the dread before she acts.
Solution-focused work would look for times when presenting already goes better and build on them. Hollis mentions no exceptions, scaling, or existing successes.
takeaway: Acceptance, values, and committed action together signal ACT: feelings need not change before behavior does.

stem: Police sergeant Ray Delgado has told consultant Aisha Mensah about freezing for a few seconds during a standoff. Aisha, who is person-centered, has reflected his feelings several times, and he agrees she has them right. Now he says, "You get it, but you're being careful with me. Straight up, what do you think of me after hearing this?" Aisha feels real respect for him. Which response best offers the facilitative condition Ray is asking for?
options: "It sounds like you feel ashamed, and worn out from doubting yourself since that night."
"What was it like for you to tell your partner about those few seconds?"
"So you've gone from questioning that night to questioning whether you still belong out there."
"I respect you, and hearing how you've faced this has deepened that for me."
rationales: Reflecting feeling conveys empathy, which Ray says he already has ("You get it"). Another reflection would confirm his sense that Aisha is holding herself back.
An open question invites more detail, and nothing in Ray's request calls for that. He has asked Aisha something, and answering with a question would avoid it.
Tying his concerns together shows that Aisha follows his meaning. Ray agrees she already understands; what he lacks is her own honest reaction.

Ray is asking for congruence, or genuineness: the person behind the role. Aisha's respect is real and he has asked for her reaction, so stating it openly is consistent with Rogers's view that the helper should be transparent rather than hide behind technique.
takeaway: When a client understands he's been heard and asks where you stand, genuineness may matter more than another reflection.

stem: Jordan Avery's written philosophy states that athletes open up to someone who shares their daily world, that lasting change usually starts in unplanned moments, and that formal sessions are a supplement. At a first meeting, a collegiate volleyball coach asks how Jordan will work with the team this season. Which description is most consistent with that philosophy?
options: "I'll be around practice and on trips, and most of my work will be brief chats."
"I'll teach skills early in the season, and players will run them without me by playoffs."
"I'll work mainly with your staff, and players will hear the ideas from their coaches."
"I'll see players by appointment, and each one will choose what we work on."
rationales: Being present in the team's everyday setting and working through short, informal contacts follows from each of Jordan's stated beliefs. Consultants' roles and methods should flow from their core beliefs about how people change.
Teaching early and fading out fits a philosophy of athlete self-reliance. Jordan's philosophy puts formal teaching second and values being there when unplanned moments arise.
Working through coaches suits a philosophy that sees them as the main influence on athletes. Jordan's rests on athletes' trust in the consultant, which this arrangement would give up.
Scheduled, player-led meetings suit a philosophy of private, self-directed work. Jordan treats formal sessions as a supplement to sharing the daily world of the team.
takeaway: A consultant's delivery style should be traceable to stated beliefs about how people change.

stem: In a video call, professional esports player Malik Haddad says that after a lost round he goes silent or snaps at teammates, as he has done for years with anyone he might disappoint. He asks how working with Ottilie Brekke will help. Ottilie uses an interpersonal process approach, which expects a client's patterns to show up in sessions too. Which explanation is most consistent with that approach?
options: "We'll spot rounds when you shook off a loss, and build on what you did then."
"We'll catch what you tell yourself after a loss, and check how well it fits the facts."
"We'll notice how you deal with people under strain, including how you deal with me."
"We'll practice letting the frustration come and go while you keep playing your game."
rationales: Building on rounds that went better is solution-focused. Ottilie's approach attends to the pattern as it unfolds between people, sessions included.
Checking self-statements against facts is cognitive-behavioral. Ottilie's approach makes his way of relating, rather than the accuracy of his thoughts, the focus.

An interpersonal process approach treats the working relationship as a live sample of the client's patterns, so what happens between consultant and client becomes material for change. Telling Malik this now sets accurate expectations.
Letting frustration come and go describes mindfulness- and acceptance-based work. It targets his inner experience, while Ottilie's approach targets how he relates to others.
takeaway: Interpersonal process work uses what happens between client and consultant as material for change.

topic: Matching a first session to readiness
stem: A high school basketball coach refers 16-year-old Devon Harris to Rachel Kim, saying Devon "refuses to do any pre-game routine." With a parent's permission and Devon's assent in place, Rachel meets him. Devon says that was true last season; since then he has made up his mind that a routine would help, tried a teammate's version once at home, and wants one in place within two weeks. Using the transtheoretical model, which focus for this first session fits Devon best?
options: Ask what he has heard about pre-game routines and what he makes of them
Weigh with him what he would gain and lose by using a routine
Work out how he will keep his routine going on trips and bad days
Help him settle on a routine and pick the game in which he'll start it
rationales: Raising awareness without pressure suits precontemplation, which is the Devon the coach describes. Devon's own account is that he has decided and has already tried a routine.
Weighing pros and cons suits the ambivalence of contemplation. Devon has made up his mind and has a time frame, so this would hold him at a point he has passed.
Protecting an established habit suits later action and maintenance. Devon does not have a routine in place yet.

Intending to act very soon and having taken a small step place Devon in preparation, where a specific plan and start point help most. His own report of readiness, rather than the coach's description, should set the session's focus.
takeaway: Let the client's current readiness, not the referral's description, set the starting point.

stem: Two consultants serve the same university. Their written philosophies list the same core beliefs about people, both name cognitive-behavioral theory, both describe themselves as collaborators with athletes, and both rely on self-talk and imagery. Yet one counts her work done when competition results improve, while the other counts it done when athletes are thriving in and out of sport. In a hierarchical view of professional philosophy, at which level do the two consultants most clearly differ?
options: Personal core beliefs and values about people
Goals that each intervention is meant to reach
Model of practice and role taken with clients
Techniques and methods used to intervene
rationales: Core beliefs sit at the base of the hierarchy, and the stem says the two lists are the same. The difference appears in the end each is working toward.
One aims at competitive results and the other at the whole person's thriving, so they differ in intervention goals. Beliefs, theory, role, and techniques are each described as shared.
Both describe themselves as collaborators, so the role each takes with athletes is the same. What differs is the outcome that each treats as success.
Both rely on self-talk and imagery, so their methods match. The same techniques are being put to different ends.
takeaway: Two consultants can share beliefs, theory, role, and techniques yet differ in what they count as success.

stem: Ben Asante works from a structured cognitive-behavioral model and has no training in other approaches. At intake, masters marathoner Ingrid Solberg, 58, asked for open-ended conversations about what running means to her as her racing years end. Ben described how he works, and they talked over whether it would suit her. After a week's thought, Ingrid tells him clearly that she still wants the open-ended kind and doesn't want to try his. What should Ben do next?
options: Give her the names of colleagues who are trained in nondirective work
Explain his structured model and ask how well it suits her aims
Begin his usual cognitive-behavioral program and review the fit with her in two weeks
Set his usual structure aside and let her lead their conversations
rationales: Ben has been transparent, the two have discussed fit, and Ingrid has made an informed choice that lies outside his training. Connecting her with someone competent in what she wants respects both her autonomy and the limits of his competence.
Explaining the model and discussing fit comes first in such cases, and it has been done. Ingrid took a week to think and gave a clear answer.
A short trial with a review is reasonable when a client is curious about it. Ingrid says she doesn't want to try his approach.
Adapting to a client's preference fits a consultant competent in both ways of working. Ben has no training outside his structured model.
takeaway: Once fit has been discussed openly and the answer is no, help the client reach someone who fits.

stem: A supervisor reviews recordings of virtual sessions between wheelchair tennis player Camila Reyes and Theo Nguyen, who identifies as person-centered. Theo is sincerely fond of Camila and equally warm after wins and losses; Camila says so and feels at ease with him. But when she describes shame at letting her coach down, he restates it as anger about the draw, much as he felt in his own playing days, and she often has to correct him. Which of Rogers's conditions is Theo most clearly failing to provide?
options: Psychological contact between consultant and client
Congruence between what he feels and shows
Accurate empathy for her frame of reference
Unconditional positive regard for her as a person
rationales: Psychological contact means the two are in a relationship in which each registers the other. Camila feels at ease and engages with Theo, so contact is present.
Congruence means the consultant's outward manner matches inner experience. Theo's fondness is sincere, so nothing suggests a front.

Theo hears Camila's shame as anger because he filters it through his own history, and she has to correct him. Empathic understanding requires sensing her experience as if it were his own without letting his experience take over.
Unconditional positive regard means acceptance that doesn't depend on how the client performs. Theo is equally warm after wins and losses.
takeaway: Warmth and sincerity don't guarantee empathy, which means grasping the client's meaning rather than one's own.

stem: Fourteen-year-old figure skater Corentin Quiroga has begun turning planned jumps into easier ones at the last moment in practice. With his guardian's permission and Corentin's assent, Grace Liu begins her assessment. Grace works from an operant behavioral perspective and wants to find out what might be maintaining the habit. Which assessment question best fits her perspective?
options: "What goes through your mind as you set up for one of those jumps?"
"What happens right after you turn a jump into an easier one?"
"Which recent practices went a little better, and what was different in them?"
"How do the adults at home and at the rink get along about your skating?"
rationales: Asking about thoughts suits a cognitive perspective. An operant perspective explains the habit by what surrounds and follows it, so thoughts are not Grace's first target.

Operant theory holds that behavior is maintained by its consequences, such as relief, praise, or escape from a fall. Asking what follows the switch looks for the reinforcer that keeps the habit going.
Asking about exceptions suits a solution-focused perspective, which builds on what works. Grace wants to know what maintains the habit.
Asking how home and rink connect suits an ecological perspective. Grace's operant perspective focuses on the events tied to the behavior itself.
takeaway: An operant assessment asks what follows a behavior, because consequences keep it going.

stem: Orchestral trumpet player Nadia Petrova tells consultant Samuel Osei that her hands shake before auditions and that her doctor has found no medical cause. She adds that the shaking has become "a whole thing" at home and in her section. Samuel works from a systems perspective and wants to understand what keeps the shaking going. Which assessment question best fits his perspective?
options: "When your hands shake, who notices first, and how do people respond?"
"When your hands shake, what do you tell yourself that it means?"
"When have your hands shaken less, and what was different that day?"
"When you try to stop the shaking, what does the effort cost you?"
rationales: A systems perspective looks for the pattern of interaction around a problem: each person's response may help maintain it. Asking who notices and how people respond traces that pattern across home and section.
Asking about the meaning she gives the symptom suits a cognitive perspective, which places the maintaining factor in her appraisal. Samuel looks for it in interactions.
Asking when the problem is smaller suits a solution-focused perspective, which looks for exceptions rather than for what maintains a problem.
Asking about the cost of control suits acceptance and commitment therapy, which targets her struggle with the symptom. Samuel's perspective focuses on what happens among people.
takeaway: Systems assessment asks how people's responses to one another keep a pattern going.

stem: A college athletic department asks Elena Vasquez why many athletes skip the injury-prevention warm-up designed by the sports medicine staff. She is building a survey on the theory of planned behavior. Her draft already asks how worthwhile athletes think the warm-up is, whether they have the time and know-how to do it, and whether they mean to do it this month. Which of the theory's constructs does she still need to cover?
options: How useful and pleasant athletes judge the warm-up to be
How easy or difficult athletes expect the warm-up to be
How strong athletes' intentions are to complete the warm-up
How much athletes sense that teammates and coaches expect it
rationales: This is the attitude component, which her question about how worthwhile the warm-up is already covers.
This is perceived behavioral control, which her questions about time and know-how already cover.
This is intention, which her question about whether athletes mean to do it this month already covers.

In the theory of planned behavior, attitudes, subjective norms, and perceived behavioral control shape intention. Her draft covers the others, so the perceived expectations of people who matter (subjective norm) are missing.
takeaway: Planned behavior needs attitudes, subjective norms, and perceived control to account for intention.

topic: Choosing the ACT process to plan around
stem: Assessment with collegiate pole vaulter Amara Diallo shows that she can watch thoughts like "I'll balk" come and go without arguing with them, lets herself feel fear on the runway, and has entered every meet on the schedule. Asked why she vaults, she shrugs: "I've done it since I was ten. I couldn't tell you what it's for anymore." Her consultant, Felix Romero, works from acceptance and commitment therapy (ACT). Which focus should the plan take first?
options: Practice treating her thoughts as passing words rather than facts
Practice making room for fear rather than pushing it away
Clarify what she wants her vaulting to be about and stand for
Commit to dates for the meets that she would rather avoid
rationales: This is cognitive defusion, for a client caught up in her thoughts. Amara already lets hers come and go without arguing.
This is acceptance, for a client who struggles against her feelings. Amara already lets herself feel fear.
Amara shows defusion, acceptance, and action but can't say what the action serves. Values clarification is the ACT process missing from the data, and it gives direction to the skills she already has.
This is committed action, for a client who knows what matters but isn't acting on it. Amara already enters every meet.
takeaway: Let the data show which ACT process is missing instead of working through them all.

stem: Firefighter Owen Gallagher used to play video games until 3 a.m. between shifts. Eight months ago he moved to an earlier bedtime with screens off, and he has kept to it nearly every free night since, sleeping well. He starts at a busier station next month, wants to hold on to what he has, and asks his consultant for a plan. Using the transtheoretical model, what should the plan focus on?
options: Learning how too little sleep affects alertness and decisions on emergency calls
Weighing what he would gain and lose by changing his bedtime habits
Choosing a start date and telling his crew about the coming change
Spotting nights when old habits could return and preparing for them
rationales: Consciousness raising suits earlier stages, when a person hasn't yet seen a reason to change. Owen changed eight months ago and sees the value.
A decisional balance suits contemplation, when a person is torn about changing. Owen has already changed and wants to keep it up.
Setting a date and making a public commitment suit preparation. Owen's new habit is eight months old.
More than six months of sustained change places Owen in maintenance, where the work is consolidating gains and preventing relapse. A busier station makes it timely to plan for high-risk nights.
takeaway: After six months of change, planning shifts from starting the behavior to protecting it.

stem: Analyst Leah Brooks has gone quiet in her trading desk's strategy meetings. She tells Hana Ito that junior staff get little airtime there, that "one bad idea and I'm finished," that she feels relief each time she stays silent, and that growing up she was praised when useful and ignored otherwise, "so I keep the real me out of it." Hana works from person-centered theory. Which interpretation of Leah's silence best fits that theory?
options: She hides who she is to meet conditions set on her worth
She treats one poor idea as proof that she would fail
She is rewarded with relief when she stays out of discussions
She has adapted to a desk where some people's ideas count less
rationales: Person-centered theory holds that people who learn their worth is conditional come to deny parts of themselves to keep others' regard. Leah's history of praise when useful, and keeping "the real me" out, fit conditions of worth and the incongruence they create.
Her "one bad idea and I'm finished" could be read as a distorted appraisal, which is the focus of cognitive therapy. Hana's theory looks at conditional regard and the hidden self.
Relief that strengthens silence is a negative reinforcement reading, which belongs to behavioral theory. Hana's theory centers on self and worth.
Attention to who gets heard is a power analysis, as in feminist theory. It fits some of the data, but Hana works from person-centered theory.
takeaway: The same data support several readings; the consultant's theory decides which one organizes the plan.

stem: Raj Patel is helping a tech company plan an employee exercise program. His theory of planned behavior survey shows that employees have paid time for it and know how to use the on-site gym, believe that managers and coworkers want them to exercise, and have weak intentions to do so. Most rate working out during the workday as unpleasant and of little benefit to them. Which planning priority best follows from these results?
options: Shorter workouts and protected calendar time that make exercise easier to fit in
Enjoyable sample classes and messages on what employees gain from exercise
Senior leaders and respected coworkers who visibly encourage staff to exercise
Planning prompts in which staff write down when and where they will exercise
rationales: Removing obstacles raises perceived behavioral control, but employees already have paid time and know-how. Control is not what holds intentions down.

Control and subjective norms are strong, so the weak link is attitude: employees expect exercise to be unpleasant and unrewarding. Positive experience and information on benefits target those beliefs, and through them intention.
Visible endorsement strengthens subjective norms. Employees already believe that managers and coworkers want them to exercise.
Writing when and where helps people who intend to act but don't follow through. These employees' intentions are weak, so there is little yet to carry out.
takeaway: Aim a planned behavior intervention at the predictor the data show is weak.

stem: Mira Hoffman, who works from a systems perspective, is asked to help a collegiate hockey team. She learns that the head coach and the starting goalie haven't spoken directly about his playing time in weeks. Each takes complaints to the assistant coach instead, who soothes both and carries messages. Tension eases for a few days after these talks, the disagreement stays unsettled, and the assistant is worn out. Which interpretation should guide Mira's plan?
options: Homeostasis, in which a group pulls back toward its usual way of working
Enmeshment, in which members become so involved that their roles blur
Triangulation, in which two people handle their tension through a third person
Circular causality, in which each person's reaction feeds the other's
rationales: Homeostasis explains a system drifting back after someone tries to change it. No one here has attempted a change; the striking feature is who carries the conflict.
Enmeshment describes overly close, blurred boundaries. The coach and goalie are avoiding each other, and their roles remain distinct.

Coach and goalie route their conflict through the assistant, which lowers tension for a while and lets the issue go unsettled. Seeing a triangle points the plan toward direct talk between the two and relief for the assistant.
Circular causality describes reactions that feed each other back and forth. The coach and goalie have little direct exchange; both go through the assistant.
takeaway: When two people send their conflict through a third, work toward direct contact between the two.

stem: Zoe Adler's written philosophy states that her role in season is that of an expert who supplies tools athletes can use the same day, and that work on how they think belongs in the off-season. In the middle of a playoff run, professional soccer player Luis Ortega reports harsh self-criticism after mistakes and wants something for tomorrow's match. Which plan is most consistent with Zoe's philosophy of practice?
options: Give Luis a short phrase to say to himself after each mistake
Have Luis log his self-criticism and weigh the evidence for it
Train Luis to observe his self-criticism without reacting to it
Help Luis talk through what his self-criticism means to him
rationales: A ready-made self-talk phrase is a same-day tool supplied by an expert, which is how Zoe defines her in-season role. Plans should follow from the consultant's philosophy, including its view of timing and role.
Logging and evaluating thoughts is cognitive restructuring, which takes repeated practice and works on how he thinks. Zoe's philosophy saves that for the off-season.
Training a new stance toward thoughts is mindfulness work built up over weeks. Luis wants something for tomorrow, and Zoe's philosophy calls for same-day tools.
Exploring personal meaning suits a person-centered philosophy. Zoe defines her in-season role as supplying tools rather than exploring how athletes think.
takeaway: A philosophy of practice guides not just which techniques to use but when to use them.

stem: Collegiate diver Bianca Moretti believed, "If I'm not calm, I'll miss the dive." Over six weeks Isaac Levin, who uses cognitive-behavioral methods, had her record the thought, weigh the evidence for it, and test it by diving while nervous, in practice and at two small meets. Away from competition she now says with conviction, "I can dive well nervous." Just before her dives at meets, though, the old idea crowds in and she "can't call up what we worked out." What should Isaac do next?
options: Have her record the thoughts she has at the pool this week
Have her weigh what supports and contradicts her belief about calm
Have her predict and then test how she dives while nervous
Have her write her conclusion on a card that she reads poolside
rationales: Recording thoughts helps identify what a client is thinking. The thought has been identified, and Bianca reports exactly what crowds in at meets.
Weighing evidence helps when the client still believes the thought. Bianca has done this and is convinced of the new conclusion.
A behavioral experiment tests a belief that talking hasn't shifted. Bianca has run those dives, at meets too, and is convinced; her trouble is recall under pressure.

Bianca has reached and believes a new conclusion but can't retrieve it at meets. A coping card is the cognitive-behavioral tool for bringing a hard-won conclusion into the situation where it's needed.
takeaway: If the new belief is sound but hard to recall under pressure, support retrieval instead of repeating the analysis.

stem: Wheelchair basketball player Kofi Boateng rates his confidence at the free-throw line 1 out of 10, though the rest of his game and his life are going well. Elif Demir, who uses a solution-focused approach, has asked him to picture the problem solved, to describe one point higher, and to recall any better spell. To each he answers, "I've got nothing." He still stays late to shoot after every practice. Which question best fits the approach now?
options: "What would you notice yourself doing if you were one point higher?"
"How have you managed to keep going through a stretch this hard?"
"When has your shooting been even slightly better than it is now?"
"If this were solved overnight, what would you notice first tomorrow?"
rationales: A next-point question helps a client define a small step. Kofi has just been asked this and could not answer.
When a client can't see exceptions or a better future, solution-focused practice turns to coping questions. Kofi's extra shooting is a strength, and this question draws out what sustains it.
An exception question finds times the problem is smaller. Elif has asked, and Kofi could recall none.
The miracle question helps a client picture a preferred future. Kofi has been asked to picture the problem solved and came up empty.
takeaway: When exceptions and future pictures come up empty, ask how the client has coped.

stem: Naomi Barrett, who works from a feminist approach, has supported a collegiate women's ice hockey team that gets worse practice slots than the men's team. Last month the players talked through how the program's rules had shaped the way they see themselves, named the inequity, planned their case, and presented it to the athletic director, who will answer in two weeks. Today they say there is nothing more to do until then, and they want to spend the hour on Saturday's opponent. Which response is most consistent with Naomi's approach?
options: Examine how the rules of their program affect how they see themselves
Work out who will raise the practice slots, with whom, and how
Focus the session on what they can control in their upcoming game
Offer to speak to the athletic director about the practice slots
rationales: Consciousness raising helps people connect personal distress to unequal conditions. These players named the inequity a month ago and acted on it.
Planning collective action empowers a team that is ready to act. The case has been planned and presented, and an answer is due.

Feminist practice treats clients as the experts on their own needs and shares power over the agenda. The players have acted on the inequity, are waiting on a set date, and have chosen how to use the hour.

Advocacy with clients' agreement can fit a feminist approach when their own voice has been shut out. These players were heard, and speaking for them now would take over a process that they're leading.
takeaway: Empowerment includes honoring a group's own decision about when to act and when to move on.

topic: When an automatic thought is accurate
stem: Military flight student Rohan Mehta tells Dana Whitaker, "I could wash out of this program." Dana, who uses cognitive methods, goes through his record with him: he has failed two check rides, and one more failure ends his training. They agree the thought is accurate. Rohan doesn't see it as a verdict on himself; he says he just has no idea how to organize the ten days before his next ride. What should Dana do next?
options: Turn to problem solving and lay out his preparation time
Ask him what in his record supports and contradicts the thought
Ask him what the thought would mean about him if it came true
Set up an experiment that tests whether the thought is accurate
rationales: When an automatic thought proves accurate, cognitive therapy moves from evaluating it to solving the problem it points to. Rohan's difficulty is organizing ten days, and he isn't drawing a harsher conclusion about himself.
Weighing evidence suits a thought that may be distorted. Dana and Rohan have gone through the record and agree the thought is accurate.
Tracing the meaning of a thought, as in the downward arrow, helps when a deeper self-judgment drives distress. Rohan says he doesn't see this as a verdict on himself.
A behavioral experiment tests a belief whose truth is uncertain. The record has already shown that this thought is accurate.
takeaway: If a worrying thought checks out as true and carries no distorted meaning, solve the problem.

stem: Masters triathlete Gwen Holloway, 61, has medical clearance and no injury. Late in races she tenses up and battles the ordinary burn in her legs, trying to make it stop, and her pace drops. She says that her thoughts don't bother her, that her mind stays on the race, and that she knows just why she competes. Pavel Novak uses acceptance and commitment therapy. Which technique best fits what Gwen describes?
options: Saying "I'm having the thought that" before what her mind tells her
Naming three sights and sounds around her at each kilometer
Writing down what she wants to stand for as a competitor
Breathing around the sensations and letting them stay as she runs
rationales: This is a defusion technique for a client caught up in thoughts. Gwen says her thoughts don't bother her.
This is a present-moment technique for a client whose attention drifts. Gwen says her mind stays on the race.
This is a values technique for a client unsure what the effort serves. Gwen knows just why she competes.

Gwen's difficulty is the struggle to get rid of ordinary discomfort. Acceptance, or willingness, means making room for such sensations while continuing to act, which frees the effort that she spends fighting them.
takeaway: Pick the ACT technique for the process that's stuck: thoughts, attention, values, or struggle with sensations.

topic: Finding the missing process of change
stem: Andre Lefebvre began exercising four times a week two months ago. He sets out his gear with phone alerts on, trains with his sister on most days, and buys himself a record after each full week. The workouts he still misses all follow tense work calls, when he turns on the television to settle himself. Lucia Ferraro is using the transtheoretical model's processes of change. Which addition best supplies the process missing from his plan?
options: Post reminders to exercise where he'll see them each evening
Arrange for a friend to join him at his weekly workouts
Swap his usual way of unwinding after work for a brisk walk
Earn a small treat for each workout that he completes
rationales: Reminders are stimulus control, which his gear and phone alerts already provide. The missed workouts come from how he settles himself, not from forgetting.
A workout partner is a helping relationship, which he already has in his sister.

Counterconditioning means substituting a healthier response for the one that competes with the new behavior. Television is how Andre settles after tense calls, and a brisk walk can take its place; cues, support, and rewards are already covered.
Rewards are reinforcement management, which his record for each full week already provides.
takeaway: Compare the processes of change already in use with the pattern of slips to see which one is missing.

stem: Collegiate rower Imani Carter arrives for a planned imagery session and tears up, saying her father was diagnosed with a serious illness on Monday. Erik Sandberg, who is person-centered, listens, reflects what he hears, and asks what she would like from today. Imani shows no signs of risk. She says she has talked with family and a campus counselor every day, doesn't want to go over it again, and would love "an hour of just rowing in my head." What should Erik do next?
options: Reflect what she is feeling and give her room to talk
Guide her through the imagery session that they had planned
Give her the details of the campus counseling service
Help her work out how to fit family visits around training
rationales: Erik has already listened and reflected, and Imani says she doesn't want to go over it again. Steering her back to it would put his idea of what she needs ahead of hers.
Person-centered work trusts the client to know what she needs. Imani has been heard, has support, and has plainly asked for the imagery, so going ahead with it is following her lead.
Offering a counseling contact helps a client who lacks support or asks for it. Imani is already seeing a campus counselor daily and shows no signs of risk.
Practical planning helps a client who is torn over logistics. Imani raises no such difficulty and has said what she wants from the hour.
takeaway: Following the client's lead can mean going ahead with the planned skill when that is what they ask for.

stem: Professional softball pitcher Rosa Jimenez says that after walking a batter she falls apart. At their third session, game charts bear her out: across eleven outings there is no exception. Each time she has responded the same way, stepping off the mound, lecturing herself, and throwing harder. Rosa wants a task for this week's games. Will Thornton uses a solution-focused approach. Which task best fits what they know?
options: Do something different after a walk, even if it seems odd
Do more of what she did in outings that went better
Notice what in her pitching she would like to keep happening
Predict before each outing how it will go after a walk, and check
rationales: With no exceptions and the same unhelpful response repeated, solution-focused practice follows the rule that if something isn't working, do something different. De Shazer's "do something different" task breaks the pattern without analyzing its cause.
Doing more of what works needs exceptions that the client can repeat. The charts show none in eleven outings.
Noticing what she wants to continue is the formula first-session task, useful when the complaint is vague. This is the third session, and the complaint is specific.
Prediction tasks help when good outings occur but the client can't explain them. Rosa's charts show no good outings after a walk.
takeaway: Solution-focused tasks follow the data: repeat what works, and when nothing has worked, do something different.

stem: Freya Lind, an elite cross-country skier, reaches each start through a settled warm-up routine, knows her focus cues for every section of the course, and writes down the lessons after each race. When something unexpected happens, such as a broken pole or a late course change, she stays rattled for several kilometers. Her consultant, Carlos Mendes, builds on Orlick and Partington's mental links to excellence. Which element should they practice next?
options: A pre-race plan for her warm-up and the final minutes before the start
A race plan with focus cues for each section
An evaluation plan for drawing lessons from races
A distraction control plan for getting back on task quickly
rationales: A precompetition plan is one of the elements, and Freya already has a settled warm-up routine. Her difficulty arises during races.
A competition focus plan is one of the elements, and Freya knows her cues for every section. Those cues don't cover what to do when something goes wrong.
Constructive evaluation is one of the elements, and Freya already writes down lessons after each race.

Successful Olympians in Orlick and Partington's study had practiced ways to refocus after distractions. Freya's preparation, focus cues, and evaluation are in place; what she lacks is a rehearsed way back when things go wrong.
takeaway: Check which mental link is missing before adding more of those that the athlete already has.

stem: Thandiwe Mokoena consults with coaches at a youth club who want players to develop composure. Her observations show that the coaches stay calm on the sideline, give warm support, and expect full effort. Players admire how calm their coaches are but say they have no idea how to do it themselves; the coaches had assumed it would rub off. Drawing on research into how Olympic champions' psychological characteristics developed, which coach action should she help them add?
options: Model the calm behavior that they want to see from players
Give players more encouragement and emotional support after losses
Teach players composure skills directly during regular practice time
Set higher expectations for players' effort and discipline at practice
rationales: Modeling is one route through which coaches influenced champions, and these coaches already do it. Players admire the calm but can't tell how to produce it.
Support from coaches featured in champions' development, and these coaches already give it warmly. It doesn't show players how to become composed.

Gould and colleagues found that coaches and parents shaped champions' psychological characteristics both directly, by teaching, and indirectly, as by modeling. The indirect route is in place here, and players need to be taught how.
High expectations featured in champions' development, and these coaches already expect full effort. Expectations don't tell players how to stay calm.
takeaway: Coaches shape mental strengths both by example and by direct teaching; add the route that's missing.
